items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In recent years Speakers have en tered into a number of agreements
that have implications for the House a nd its members. On 24 March 2004 the House
noted a report of the Privileges Committee on its consideration of a draft agreement on
policing functions within the parliament ary precincts. Following the Privileges
Committee’s report, the Speaker and the Commissioner of Police signed a formal
agreement, which was presented to the House on 24 June 2004. The agreement
continues until termination, but is required to be reviewed every 3 years and may be
amended by mutual agreement of the two parties. A revised agreement was signed on
12 December 2007. A further review is now due.
On 7 November 2006 the Speaker presented to  the House a paper setting out interim
procedures for the execution of search wa rrants on premises occupied or used by
members of Parliament, and indicated to the House that she would seek to have the
Privileges Committee consider it once the po lice investigation into the activities of
Taito Phillip Field and any consequent action were completed. A final order for
repayment was made on 3 September 2012, and the proceedings are now at an end.
On 21 December 2010 I entered into a draft memorandum of understanding with the
New Zealand Security Intelligence Serv ice on the collection and retention of
information on members of Parliament, th e need for which arose from a 2009 report
from the Inspector-General of Intelligence  and Security, following complaints from
members.
All three of these agreements have the potential to raise issues affecting the
privileges of the House. Consequently, I have determined that they involve a question of
privilege, and therefore the question stands referred to the Privileges Committee.
Businesses—Government Initiatives to Support
1. MAGGIE BARRY (National—North Shore)  to the Minister of Finance: What
measures is the Government taking to encour age businesses to invest, grow and create
jobs?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: A number of measures to support
business confidence, because it is businesse s that make the decisions to invest and
employ. These include reforming the tax syst em to shift incentives towards working,
saving, and investing, and away from borro wing, consumption, and over-investment in
housing. We are also focusing on a faster path back to surplus to enable lower interest
rates for longer, and to improve productivit y, and, more important, quality of public
5266 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Sep 2012
services, and we are also continuing to revi ew regulation and legislation where we have
evidence that it is imposing unnecessary costs or inhibiting investment decisions.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: As part of the Government building a more productive and
competitive economy, which legislation is being reviewed?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We have, for instance, reviewed and amended the Securities
Act and the Employment Relations Act, a nd also, quite extensively, the building and
construction legislation. We have re moved 170 excessive regulations. We are
undertaking phase two of reviewing the Res ource Management Act to ensure that it
reflects broader community expectations about  job growth as well as the environment.
Job growth is as important to the sustainabi lity of our communities as the environment,
and the two are certainly not mutually exclusive.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: How does the Resource Management Act impact on investment?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government has over the last few years made a number
of changes to the Resource Management Act,  since it is the pr incipal regulator of
environmental impacts. A consistent th eme of discussions with homeowners,
particularly those who want to get into their first home, and investors is that they can be
frustrated by the costs of delay and also by the uncertainty create d by that delay. Our
experience is that investors are willing to trade off limits on development and economic
opportunity in return for cer tainty around Resource Manage ment Act decision-making,
and that will be part of the Government ’s consideration in the second phase of
reviewing the Resource Management Act.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What effect have the changes th e Government has already made to
the Resource Management Act had on investment?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Probably the change that has had the most impact is to set a
9-month limit for consenting projects of national significance through the
Environmental Protection Authority. This has given the proponents of large-scale
projects, including the Governme nt with its transport projects, much more certainty
about the time frame for getting agreement on those projects, and is reducing the costs
of what would otherwise have been very long delays. This, of course, encourages those
who do have larger-scale pr ojects to look more favourab ly on those investments,
because they will lead to more jobs.
Hon John Banks—Confidence and Electoral Returns
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement given in answer to Oral Question No 2 on 1 May 2012, “my chief
of staff spoke with Hon John Banks and sought an assurance from him that he had fully
complied with the requirements of the Local  Electoral Act in respect of donations. Mr
Banks gave his assurance during the phone call and stated that he was not aware that Mr
Dotcom had made the donation to his mayoral campaign”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that for a Minister to enjoy his
confidence, “The test is: has he misled me?”

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he aware of the sworn statem ent from Gregory Towers, a partner
at Simpson Grierson, who said that Mr Banks told him in February this year, when Mr
Banks was a Cabinet Minister, that he could not assist Mr  Dotcom in getting medical
attention in prison, because “that may backfire on Kim if it became known about the
election support.”?
18 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5267

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have not read the report, but I have seen media reports. What
I am aware of is that that is a statemen t from Mr Towers, not a statement from Mr
Banks.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he aware of the dinner Mr Banks had with Kim Dotcom where
Kim Dotcom offered him $50,000, to which he replied “No, not one cheque. Write two
cheques out for $25,000 each.”, as cited in the sworn statement of Kim Dotcom’s
security guard?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I am not aware of the speci fic dinner that the member is
talking of, although I am aware that Mr Banks  had dinner with Mr Dotcom. I am also
aware that under the rules of the existing legisl ation it is quite within  the rules to solicit
cheques and donations on such a basis and comply with the law.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Can he assure the House that the changes to the Local Electoral Act
that he is proposing will address the issues raised in the police files on John Banks?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I have not read the re port, but I can say that this
Government will tidy up that legislation, where that Government  failed. A couple of
years ago the Labour Party was not worried about this issue—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That was a pretty straight
question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The—[Interruption] Order! I think the question was answered, but I
think the territory the Prime Minister was about to go into then was probably beyond the
question asked.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: How can he be 100 percent sure  that the new amendments will
address those issues when he actually has not read the police files on John Banks?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am certainly well and truly aw are of the failings of electoral
law. Funnily enough, so is the Labour Party, because if I was to quote from Prime
Minister Helen Clark, she said through a spokeswoman that the electoral law was
“confusing, contradictory and needed to be reviewed.” Guess what! Helen Clark and I
worked it out. The shame is that Helen Clark did nothing about it.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Why does the Prime Minister refuse  to read the police files on John
Banks?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because it is not my practice to  go and read police files. This
will come as a great shock to the member, but the police are independent in New
Zealand. They do their own investigations, and guess what! This is  the bit that the
Labour Party is not quoting. Guess what! Th e police said that there was insufficient
evidence to prosecute—by the way, no case.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: How can he continue to claim th at John Banks did not mislead him,
given that Mr Banks claimed that he was not aware of the donations from Kim Dotcom,
in spite of the fact that he solicited the donation at a dinner at Dotcom’s house; asked
that the donation be split in half so he  could claim it was anonymous; thanked Mr
Dotcom for the donations during a phone call; and, as recently as on 8 February this
year, declined to assist Mr Dotcom on the basis he had donated to Mr Banks’
campaign?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am confident of two things: firstly, that my chief of staff
spoke to Mr Banks’ office and sought an assu rance that he had fu lly complied with the
requirements of the Local Electoral Act, a nd, secondly, that he was not aware that Mr
Dotcom had made donations. Many of the thin gs that the member is now claiming are
within the law. By the way, there are many older members of this Parliament—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I think there has been sufficient
answer.
5268 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Can the Prime Minister remember saying “This is not a Prime
Minister in control. It is a Prime Minister in damage control … She should now act over
Mr Field. Why are we waiting, Prime Minister? … Helen Clark is only interested in
protecting her slim majority in Parliament .”, and what has changed, other than the
Prime Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: A couple of things. First, yes, I remember making that
statement. Secondly, I am not surprised Trevor Mallard is on feet, because, quite
frankly, David Shearer is going about as well—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! Look—[Interruption] Order! I ask the
House to settle down a moment. This is not going to be easy if it gets too testy.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Is the Prime Minister still sa tisfied and will he rely on the
police conclusion when the evidence now s hows that John Banks lied to his chief of
staff and/or the media on this matter; if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The matter does not show that Mr Banks lied to my chief of
staff—quite the contrary. Mr Banks complied with the law. You see, the Labour Party
cares about the law today, but it did not care about it enough to change it. If you cared
so much a while ago, change the law back then.
Hon John Banks—Police Investigation into Electoral Returns
3. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by his statement that Hon John Banks has “got  a version of events, others have got a
different version. It’s not for me to forensically go through that”; if so, whose job is it to
hold his Ministers to account for the veracity of their statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is referring to statements made
to the police, whose job it is to assess the evidence before them. I have no responsibility
for assessing evidence given to the New Zealand Police. However, I would note that the
police decided there was “insufficient eviden ce to consider a prosecution under section
134(1) of the Local Electoral Act …”.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why does the Prime Minister be lieve John Banks when John Banks
says that he did not read his donations declaration even though he signed it, despite
comments by John Banks’ ministerial press se cretary that he did read the documents
and that his campaign treasurer went over the declaration with him?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because I accept the Minister at his word.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I seek leave to table an email exchange dated 13 September 2012
between John Banks’ press secretary and a New Zealand Herald journalist where the
press secretary first claims that John Banks re ad the declaration and later clarifies that
John Banks’ campaign treasurer went over the form with John Banks.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that do cumentation. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Documents, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is it a new policy of the Prime Minister that Ministers are not
responsible for documents that they sign, and is this a new “don’t read, don’t care”
defence on “Planet Key”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No. I refer the member to the fact that the document was
signed when he was not a Minister.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will homeowners on “Planet Key” now be allowed to default on
their mortgages and then claim it is OK b ecause they did not read the documents; will
business people on “Planet Key” now be allowed to sign illegal—[Interruption]
18 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5269

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I apologise to the member. I could not hear her question and
it is important I can. I invite her to start again. Members must make it possible for the
Speaker to hear the questions.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will homeowners on “Planet Key” now be allowed to default on
their mortgages and then claim it is OK b ecause they did not read the documents; will
business people on “Planet Key” now be allo wed to sign illegal contracts under his new
“don’t read, don’t care” defence?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not know so much about “Planet Key”, but my
expectations are it would be a lovely place to live, it would be beautifully governed,
golf courses would be plentiful, people woul d have plenty of ho lidays to enjoy their
time, and what a wonderful place it would be. But I would expect people on such a
place—referred to as nirvana—to comply with the law, and that is what Mr Banks did.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Metiria Turei. [Interruption] Order! I want to hear this question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Thank you. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I want to hear the question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is there one standard for ordina ry New Zealanders, who are legally
responsible for any statement or contract that  they sign up to, and another for the Prime
Minister’s Ministers, who can put their name to whatever fa lsehood they like as long as
they live on “Planet Key”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The question here is whether Mr Banks complied with the
law, and it is our belief he did. As I was saying ear lier, the law prior to the changes for
central government would have seen many memb ers of this Parliament do things that
would be illegal today but were legal back then. There are also successful candidates
who have funnelled money through trusts, for instance, which are legal when it comes
to the law. I expect people to comply with the law. That is pretty simple.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Metiria Turei.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I want to hear this question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will his Government now be changing the law so that enforcement
agencies such as the Serious Fraud Office or the police can also apply his new “don’t
read, don’t care” defence, or, again, is it only Ministers on “Planet Key” who are
entitled to that privilege?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is missing the point. The point is whether the
member complied with the law. The member may not like—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I apologise to the right honourable Prime Minister, but I will
not tolerate that kind of interjection. The member will not do that any further. He knows
that it is contrary to the Standing Orders of this House to accuse another member of
lying.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will not entertain a point of order on the matter. I have ruled on
that matter. There can be no interjections a ccusing any member of th is House of lying.
If the member wishes to raise a point of order, he may, but it will be on a different
matter.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I would like to refer you to Hansard, Volume 633, at page
5055 and the comments that day of Dr the Hon Lockwood Smith.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will look at them when I have  time. Supplementary question,
Metiria Turei.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The Prime Minister had not
completed his answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the Prime Minister had long enough to answer it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Oh, I was enjoying myself but.
5270 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Given the nature of the supplem entary question, I think the Prime
Minister had long enough to deal with it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Can I ask the Prime Minister why a police incapacity
because something was statute-barred at the time is being interpreted by him as being a
compliance with the law by Mr Banks?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: First, it is my belief that th e member complied with the law,
because that is the assurance he gave me. S econdly, I refer to the press release from the
police, who have said quite clearly that they had decided there was insufficient evidence
to consider a prosecution. Thirdly, there are actually other examples in this House,
which I will not bother going into, but there are some very esteemed members who have
often said that looking at things, even when there was a prima facie case, would be
trivial to pursue.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I asked the Prime
Minister about a specific position in the law th at the police have taken. They said that
this matter was statute-barred and therefore they could not take it any further. I—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Where is the point of order?

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is he now the Speaker of the House?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I am now on my feet. I am not sure
how—[Interruption] Order! The Leader of the House should know better than that. He
does not need to lower himself to that level. It does not help the order of the House for
the member to do that. The member asked a qu estion, and it would appear from what he
is trying to say in the point of  order he is raising that he  wants the Prime Minister to
give a legal opinion. If I am wrong on that, I am happy to hear the member further, but
it must relate to order and not the quality of the answer given by the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am not raising a
question about the quality of the answer. I am asking a question about whether the
Prime Minister even addressed the question I asked.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: To save time, I am going to allow the member to repeat his
question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. Can I ask the Prime
Minister why he is taking the police incapacity that they expressed—because any action
by them against Mr Banks would have been  statute-barred—to mean that Mr Banks
complied with the law?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not; I am taking the member at his word.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Frankly, I think that if
the Prime Minister can get away with th at, he might as well just get up and say
“Rhubarb!”, because—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, no. Order! [ Interruption] Order! No, no, the House will settle
down. Order! I am on my feet, and the Hous e will settle down. The question asked why
the Prime Minister was not taking what the member alleges in a report in respect of
something being statute-barred and, instead, was choosing to interpret that the member
has not broken the law. The Prime Ministe r’s answer to that was that he took the
member’s word that he had not broken the law, and that is an answer to that question. I
think when one analyses the question asked and the answer given, it may not have been
exactly the answer being sought, but I have to accept that it is an answer to the question
why the Prime Minister has done that.
Offenders, Serious—Proposed Public Protection Order
4. MARK MITCHELL (National—Rodney)  to the Minister of Justice : What
steps is the Government taking to better pr otect the public from imminent and serious
sexual and violent offenders?
18 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5271

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Today I have introduced the Public
Safety (Public Protection Orders) Bill. It in troduces a civil detention regime to protect
the public from the most serious sexual and violent offenders. Public protection orders
may be imposed by the High Court, at the request of the Chie f Executive of the
Department of Corrections, for offenders who have served a prison sentence for a
serious sexual or violent offence and who still have a high risk of imminent and serious
sexual and violent offending. This Governme nt is committed to delivering on its
election promise to keep the public safe from the worst sexual and violent offenders.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: How will the civil regime be managed?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: It is anticipated that only between five and 12 offenders
over a 10-year period would meet the legal te st as posing a very high risk of serious
sexual or violent offending. Offenders will und ergo a comprehensive risk assessment to
be put before the court. The High Court will determine whether the offender meets the
test for imposing an order. Individuals subject to a public protection order will be
housed in a residence located within the secure perimeter of a prison and monitored by
staff. Conditions within the residence will be monitored by independent inspectors and
the Ombudsman. Each resident will have a management plan that  will set out any
restrictions that they are s ubject to, as well as any identified needs. This detention
regime is protective rather than punitive. Residents will have as many of the normal
civil rights of ordinary citizens as possi ble without endangering the community. Public
protection orders will be subj ect to annual review by a revi ew panel comprising judges,
parole board members, and psychiatrists or registered psychologists.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: How do public protection orders differ from other regimes for
managing offenders on release from prison?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Extended supervision orders and preventive detention are
not sufficient to protect the public from these very serious offenders. Extended
supervision orders, which are set when an offender is released, can be made for up to 10
years for child sex offenders. They provide fo r an individual to be monitored and/or
accompanied at all times. However, their conditions must eventually be removed.
Public protection orders might be made for some offenders who are already subject to—

items.speaker: David Clendon
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is question time. What we
are hearing is actually a first readi ng speech on a bill that was tabled today—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order and it has some merit. Question time
is not a time to invite Ministers to give fi rst reading speeches, as the member has just
said. We will go on to Question No. 5.
Hon John Banks—Police Investigation into Electoral Returns
5. GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister :
Does he stand by his statement in answer to Supplementary Question No 3 in Oral
Question No 2 on 1 May 2012, “The test is wh ether the Minister co rrectly applied and
did everything in accordance with the law. I have received an assurance he did”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, because such an assurance was given
at the time.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is he aware that section 134 of the Local Electoral Act, which is
the law referred to in the primary question, covers two offences relating to the provision
of a false return: the first,  section 134(1), which is about knowingly furnishing a false
return, and the second, section 134(2), where it  is an offence to submit a false return
unless there is proof that there was no intent  to conceal facts, and where all reasonable
steps had been taken to ensure the information in the return was accurate?
5272 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is he further aware that in pa ragraph 39 of the police criminal
assessment report of the John Banks investigatio n police conclude that their analysis of
Mr Banks’ return was that it was a false return, in respect of his return of expenses and
donations for the 2012 mayoral election?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: If the member says so, and I am aware also that there was
insufficient evidence to consider a prosecution.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is he aware that in paragraph 40 of the police criminal assessment
report in the John Banks investigation police conclude that as a result of the return being
false the law was breached and the elements  for a prosecution were met under section

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and I just point out to the member that there are no
charges being laid against Mr Banks. He has complied with the law.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of the police finding that John Banks had breached the
law and that the elements for a prosecution had been met under section 134(2), why is
he arguing that John Banks has done everything in accordance with the law?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because that fact is not proven.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: If the test for John Banks retain ing his confidence is that he has
done everything in accordance with the law,  why will he not read a report from the
police that says that Mr Banks breached the law?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because I do not need to. The te st is whether I can rely on the
member’s word, and he has given me an assu rance that he met the law. The police have
quite clearly said there was insufficient evid ence. There is a statute of limitations, and
he has complied with the law.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is the Prime Minister telling th e people of New Zealand that his
test is not whether a Minister broke the law, but whether the Minister got away with it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, the test is whether the member complied with the law.
The member did.
Conservation Land—Milford Dart Tunnel Proposal
6. EUGENIE SAGE (Green) to the Minister of Conservation: Has she considered
making the decision herself on Milford Dart Ltd’s concession application for a private
bus tunnel, rather than delegating it to a De partment of Conservation manager; if not,
why not?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I have considered it and

consider the decision to grant the Kaituna dam proposal during the final term of the

others, delegated from the former Minister to the department.

Welfare Reforms—Social Security (Benefit Categories and Work Focus)
Amendment Bill
8. Dr JIAN YANG (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : What
changes will the Social Secu rity (Benefit Categories and Work Focus) Amendment Bill
make to the welfare system?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We are making
changes to New Zealand’s welfare system and turning it into one that has an active and
work-focused investment approach. The bill has been introduced to the House and is
expected to be read within the next couple of weeks.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What changes are being made to the current benefit categories?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: There will be three new main benefit types, which will
replace the current seven. Jobseeker suppor t will be for those actively seeking and
available for work. Those numbers from the unemployment benefit will go up to about
135,000, as we include those on the sickness  benefit and those on the DPB whose
youngest children are 14 years or over. The new sole parent support, which will go
down, because it has got those people who have their youngest children aged 14 or
younger, will have around 88,000 people on it, on today’s numbers. The new supported
living payment is for people significantly rest ricted by sickness, injury, or disability.
However, it will go up, because it will also  include those who are on the domestic
purposes benefit caring for sick or infirm, which is for those looking after someone who
would otherwise require hospital care.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: How will the changes ensure a greater work focus?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We are placing a greater focus on work. The new
jobseeker support will include those capable of work and also those who are temporarily
exempt but soon will be able to work. Thos e currently on the sickness benefit will be
now included in the jobseeker support, and will be assessed through their work capacity.
I think the main difference is that we are looking at what people can do, instead of what
they cannot, and then wrappi ng the supports round them so that they can get back to
work quickly.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Will she guarantee every child in the home of someone who is

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT

I have always been quite clear. The social ob ligations say that we want to have children
in early childhood education, we want kids who are school aged to  be at school, we
want them to be enrolled with a general pr actitioner, and we want them to get those
sorts of obligations there. If  they cannot becaus e there are barriers  or there are not
places, then we will make sure that they  are acknowledged, and they will not be
sanctioned or penalised for th at. We also know that there are empty spaces in early
5276 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Sep 2012
childhood centres that are not being taken up by children who are around that area and
who would hugely benefit from that. So we want to support them into it.

Student Loans—Changes
11. SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki) to the Minister of Revenue : How
has the Government made the student loan scheme more affordable for taxpayers?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: The Government is committed not
only to making the scheme more affordable but  also to keeping student loans interest-
free. Through a number of measures that we have taken since coming to office we have
been able to reduce the cost  to taxpayers of student loans—the write-off—from around
48c in the dollar by 19 percent to now just 39c  in the dollar. These savings allow us not
only to improve our overall fiscal position but also to reinvest in quality tertiary
education for future students.
Simon O’Connor: What actions has this Government taken to make the student loan
scheme more affordable?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: A number of actions have been taken. The most dramatic
would be the announcement in August 2010 of a pilot programme to recover debt from
overseas-based borrowers. That programme to date has brought in repayments of over
$32 million, with a further nearly $3 million under payment arrangement. We have also
reduced lending to students who are less like ly to repay, including the introduction of
requirements for academic performance, set limits on total support to encourage
students to complete their study on time, and limited lending to groups who are less
likely to pay back. And we have stopped le nding to students who are in default on
previous student loans. All of these moves he lp us not only to rec over debt that is due
but also to make the scheme far more affordable.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received letters from Ca therine Delahunty and from the Hon
Lianne Dalziel seeking to debate under Standing Order 386 the Government’s proposed
changes to education in Chri stchurch, Selwyn, and Waimakarir i. This is a particular
case of recent occurrence. The Government ’s announcement was, in fact, not publicly
released until after the House sat last T hursday, although there were earlier media
reports. It involves ministerial responsibi lity. Although the announcement is a proposal
for the future direction, and a detailed progr amme of engagement is being developed,
the proposal is an important one and foresh adows developments of very considerable
public interest. Given the significance of the matter, I consider it important enough to
warrant the immediate attention of the H ouse by way of an urge nt debate. The two
applications are not identical, but they relate to the same matter. As Catherine
Delahunty lodged her application first, I call upon her to m ove that the House take note
of a matter of urgent public importance.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: T ēnā koe. I move, That the House take
note of a matter of urgent public importance . The Christchurch educational renewal
plan is a plan for cluster l earning—or is it a cluster bomb?  This education plan has a
context that has to be acknowledged as a terrible natural disa ster now made more
complex by a very difficult response by th e Government, and there is deep mistrust
between Christchurch communities around de mocracy and around issues of education.
So we are looking at a stre ssed community who are aski ng for a logical and fair
response to a natural disaster. Instead ther e are going to be 13 school closures and 18
mergers, and people are very concerned about their ability to influence this—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would members
carrying on private conversations  like to take them outside the House. I am trying to
listen to the honourable member Catherine Delahunty.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: —and about what is the underlying agenda behind
this. That is why we already have an online petition by people concerned about children,
we have had public meetings al ready referred to in this House today, and we have a
rally tomorrow and Saturday in Christc hurch by a community who are very, very
concerned about both democracy in education and Christchurch people, who have had it
up to their necks with stress, with change, with instability, and with shock.
The Christchurch Press has made some interesting comments today, quoting other
people from that city, quoting principals, parents, and teachers about what is actually
going on for them right at this moment. As one principal said to their children, “You
have been through enough.” We are not deny ing the need for change. It would be
foolish to pretend that anything can go back to the way it was. We are not denying the
importance of reassessing education, becau se it is an opportunity to do so, but,
unfortunately, what has come out of the renewa l plan in the context of the mistrust that
we exist in has not been successful to date. It is very unfortunate  what happened last
week. It is very unfortunate that the way in  which the plan was la unched created, if you
like, an earthquake of its own. It is not being made up by pe ople in this House; it is
5280 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012
being communicated to us strongly, to all of us who are open to hearing it, that there are
real problems.
This is an issue of education as well as location, and that is why I am standing here in
support of the members of this  Parliament from Christchurch, from my party, who have
told me that they are flooded with emails from local people, as I am myself as an
education spokesperson. And all of this is occurring in a city that has been shattered and
is seeking hope and regeneration, in a city where facilities such as schools have been the
key support for the devastation of those commu nities, where local really matters more
than anywhere else. I myself , having spent time in Aranui during the earlie st days in
February, saw the role of t hose schools. I walked those streets, and I know nothing
compared with those communities who are saying: “We want change, but we want it on
our own terms.”, and I think that is a fair call.
Many of these schools have been the single st able factor in the children’s lives. Their
parents may have lost their jobs, their pare nts may have lost their home, and they may
have been moving around their suburb. They  may have been through all kinds of
changes. And, for children who are young, they  may have lost the certainty that the
earth actually supports us. Now the school, whic h has been their key place of reference
and source of resources, may be going to clos e. Maybe some of them need to. If you
take the example of Le Bons Bay School on Banks Peninsula where the predicted roll
growth is something like six, there is a logi c to it, and they support it. But if you take
Aranui and the Wainoni area a nd some of the intermediate s, there are real problems
with this renewal plan.
Many of the schools are asking us to raise issues about the real agenda. For many
people the idea of super-sizing is not logical.  It smacks more of what Naomi Klein calls
shock doctrine post-disaster reorganising than  of a plan based on the educational needs
of some of our youngest citizens. A core issu e for people is trust. How can they support
and trust a Government that has alrea dy attacked Environment Canterbury and
cancelled the local body electi on, and now is saying it is going close 13 schools and
merge 18 when the criteria have not been made clear?
What happened last Thursday did nothing to  reassure anybody that they are going to
be heard. The possible option of merging Sh irley Boys High School with Christchurch
Boys’ High School—although some say it will ne ver happen and it was never meant to
happen—is a good example of how,  if you put up an option th at is clearly a worst-case
scenario from those schools’ point of view, you will get that kind of reaction.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: So the renewal plan—sorry, Mr Speaker—is
actually putting up options that have, perhaps,  made the situation even more fraught,
which is really unfortunate, so we have ha d a lot of principals speaking out and being
very concerned. Because of the level of stress, people will ta ke the worst-case scenario
from their point of view. They will not just jump on the fact that it may be just an
option. I think that is why there has been so much concern.
The other issue is educational reform. What  the Government is asking us to do is
trust it on education. Well, I am sorry, but we have been in this House for a number of
years seeing national standards imposed on schools, whether they liked it or not. We
have seen the whole issue of class size turn ing into a ludicrous debacle, then we have
the bizarre spectre of experimental, id eological charter schools, and people in
Christchurch—and I have been there and at tended public meetings on those issues—do
not trust that this renewal plan is not connect ed to that agenda. In fact, the renewal plan
is explicit about taking opportunities, but for whom, and for whose benefit, is what the
people of Christchurch who are affected by the potential closures would like to know.
18 Sep 2012 Urgent Debates 5281
So what are the criteria? We were told la st week there are three—that there is
demographics, earthquake damage, and al so a quiet mention of educational
achievement. We would like to know what that means. What is meant by judging a
school on the third one? If those schools are being closed because they are failures, then
that needs to be put up front so those school s can challenge that, because it is a very
interesting criterion to use. So whatever , we need to examine those three things.
Demographics—there is a huge debate about demographics in Chri stchurch right now.
There is a huge debate as to whether the 4,500 or so students who have left will return
during the rebuild. There is a big debate about what is happening in early childhood
education. There is a considerable debate about what is happening in terms of the
buildings.
Some of the schools—as the Hon Lianne Dalziel just pointed out in her question—do
not have damage. So if they do not have a demographic co llapse and they do not have
damage, then it is very difficult for them to accept the rationale. If the rationale is they
are failing students, then let us go there for a moment. If they are failing students such
as M āori and Pacific students, then let us go there for a moment, because the plan is
very strong on that. Of course, I myself am ve ry interested in that discussion, but what I
am hearing from the two kura is that they ar e going to be merged ag ainst their will if
this goes ahead. The two kura are in the paper today saying they are actually going to
the Waitangi Tribunal to lodge a complaint about what they describe as a new round of
colonisation, which is hardly to the benefit of M āori students who are asking for the
choice of having two kura. These two kura are very different from each other and have
asserted that they do not want to be put together.
Te Whānau Tahi in Spreydon and Te Kura Whakapumau i te Reo T ūturu ki Waitaha
are actually complaining that they are going to be merged, when they come from really
different cultures. They compared themselves with Catholics and Jews and said it is like
saying that they should all be in one school , which is an interesting comparison. But
what I think they are really saying is: “Just because we’re M āori, don’t say we have to
merge. If you’re serious about lifting the achie vement issues, if you really want to talk
to us, be really explicit a bout these educational criteria  that you’re applying in the
renewal plan. Don’t just say it is demographics, don’t just sa y it is geotechnical, unless
you have finished the work.” We have got a situation where at Shirley Boys High
School, for example, and at other sites, the work is not actu ally finished, yet the options
are being put up that they have got to be moved. So it has created this huge level of
confusion.
It was never going to be easy, and I am not  saying the Government had an easy task,
but what is interesting is what we are hearing back from communities—and parents, in
particular—about how they see the consultation to date. So 544 people were involved in
the consultation, and many of them emphasi sed points that I believe have been
manipulated, such as the word “school” as  “hub”. If you read th e analysis of the
summary of the submissions, what you are he aring is not that people want bigger
schools, but what they want is that if their existing local school can be rebuilt, if there is
sufficient logic, and if they agree with it, that they have more services available on those
sites, which is actually a hub, but not necessa rily to be merged with bigger schools,
because bigger is not always better.
There are a huge number of issues that I would like to canvass: issues around early
childhood and the concerns around waiting lists that already exist, and issues around
school transport in a city that is already really di fficult in terms of transport. The rural
schools, such as Duvauchelle School and Okains Bay School are raising concerns
because they do not necessarily want to be  merged with Akaroa Area School. There are
issues around unfinished reports and all kind s of community issues. I went to Banks
5282 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012
Peninsula recently and I saw the size of some  of those schools. For some of them there
is logic to the mergers, but for others there is definitely not. The intermediate parents
and teachers have raised a lot of issues, because they think there is actually an agenda
around it. There are core issues around what is really going on with the plan.
Renewal is about the right of education, for professionals, parents, and teachers to
talk about the kind of hope  they want for their city—and they did that. They
participated. But many of th em are now reacting and saying that they are not actually
happy with what is being proposed. I have ma ny quotes in front of me from parents
saying things like “This has added to our uncertainty.”, “E very person we have spoken
to is furious with having something else ‘done to us’ by this Government.”, “The
schools have been a real focus of our community. With this side of the city in a constant
state of flux, they have been the rocks of  our community. By offering the children
something normal and stable and predictable, that’s what’s been important.”, and “The
communication and transparency has been co nfused, contradictory, and amateurish.”
“There has been a lack of”—this is quo ting from parents—“compassion or empathy.”
Other concerns are that consultation is a me re talking shop: “To be honest, there will be
a further push to leave Christchurch.” And one of the last comments that parents sent to
me was: “Don’t experiment with people in vu lnerable situations. Don’t experiment with
their children’s future.”
They are worried about charter schools.  They are worried about super-sized
environments. They know there has to be change , but they want the plan to reflect what
they are saying about local resilience and local power. Because if  there is one thing
people care about—and it is obvious  in the analysis of submi ssions—it is that they care
about their local cultures, a nd their local, very specifi c traditions. The people on the
west side are very concerned, but the peopl e on the east side have been through far
worse. So if there is a logic to making change, they have to have buy-in, they have to be
negotiated with in a way that is respectful for them.
Unfortunately, the launch was a really bad be ginning to a very di fficult process, and
it is really, really important that from here on there is a constructive engagement about
the criteria. So the demogra phics, the issues around whethe r it is building damage or
not, and the issue particularly around the ed ucation agenda—whether  it is failure or
whether it is underachievement or what that means—has to be made explicit to those
communities, because they are asking to know “What have we done wrong? Why are
children going to have to move?”. I think if you are going to talk about closing a school,
even not in a disaster zone, it is always very  emotional, it is always very sensitive. If
you are going to do that, you have to say you take the community with you.
There is a lot of wonderful rhetoric and there is all this wording about dual shifts and
recapitalisation, but it sounds more like de-cap italisation and decapitation. We have to
be more careful than this, because I do not think that the people of Christchurch who are
writing petitions and who are holding public  meetings are being manipulated from

items.speaker: Wellington. What they are saying is
items.text: “We liv e here. We want more dialogue. We want
to be part of the decision making and we want educational change to be based on the
robust and resilient issues that we actually live wit h.” And everybody like me who
comes from a small community knows what a school can be. If it is down to six, close
it, but if it is not, if it is an intermedia te like Chisnallwood, which is actually seen as
highly successful by its community, then we ha ve to make a better argument than say a
whole lot of rhetoric about consolidation, rejuvenation, with lots of lovely, shiny
documents, and lots of beautiful words. Bu t in the end, people who are traumatised and
children who are traumatised need a great deal  of care and there needs to be more care
than was shown last week. I appreciate the difficulty of what is trying to be done, but
18 Sep 2012 Urgent Debates 5283
hope is based on respect, and respect must be based on listening to the people on the
ground. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Huri noa i
tō tātou Whare, t ēnā tātou katoa. New Zealand has one of  the best and top-performing
education systems in the world. That has not happened by accident but by design, nor
can it be sustained without constant atten tion and innovation. Our ch allenge is always
how we can do what we do well even better,  while constantly looking for opportunities
to improve where we must. New Zealand must  continue to transform its most potent
resource, our people, through the power of  education, to grow our productivity and
economy, and to strengthen the social and cultural fabric of our society.
The terrible tragedy of the earthquakes, and the ongoing costs of all its measures, has
forced upon the people of the greater Christchurch, Waimakariri, and Selwyn areas both
its consequences and its oppor tunities, and upon the peopl e of New Zealand a willing
obligation to support. Rebuilding Christchurch  is one of four Government priorities.
Rebuilding the greater Christchurch area restores the economic pivot of the South Island
and the society and culture of its communitie s. Education not just for now but for a
strong future is a critical pa rt of the investment that ou r Government is making. So on
13 September, together with my honourable  colleague the Hon Gerry Brownlee, we
announced a $1 billion investment in the education provisions for the greater
Christchurch, Waimakariri, and Selwyn ar eas. That $1 billion will, over 10 years,
rejuvenate, restore, and cons olidate the network for educat ion options for our youngest
learners to our oldest.
We cannot simply put back what was ther e before. We must also make system
improvements. From the consultations we we re told that people wanted a mix of both
tradition and newer 21 st century options, diversity of  choice, and more equitable
education outcomes. The operational real ities of post-quake Christchurch, the
experience of sharing and colla boration, and the innovation th at has arisen have also
provided insights for ongoing provision. As we embark on this third stage of
consultation about educational renewal, I wa nt to take the opportunity of once again
thanking schools, their boards, and their princi pals for the leadership that they have
shown, and to once again highlight the trem endous success that the senior secondary
school students of the region showcase. Some schools have reported an increase of up to
15 percent in National Certificate of E ducational Achievement achievements and a
quarter of last year’s top scholars came from Christchurch schools.
So how do we both build on that success and i nvest in raising that success for five
out of five learners? Well, in  October last year we began the first round of consultation
by using an online survey, forums, and inte ractive small and public meetings on the
future shape of education provision. From  the over 200 responses we received, we
published Directions for Education Rene wal in Greater Christchurch . In May this year
we produced yet another document, which sets  out further provision,  but this time on
the specifics. We published in July the analysis of over 550 submissions, and in
September we published the opportunities for innovation. All of these together provide
the context for the third phase of consultation, which we embarked on last week.
The announcements included the $1 billion investment we are making over a 10-year
period in 41 learning community clusters, co mprising all of the learning options in a
geographic community. These clusters provide the opportunity for those communities to
consider what they th ink is their best opti on, and to put fo rward their cluster plan. In
addition, I announced three categor ies: restore, consolidate,  and rejuvenate. They are
based on the level of activity and the level of engagement that we anticipate will be
necessary for all of those schools. I announ ced that of the 215 sc hools, 42 have firm
proposals for a change of status, from closure,  to merger, to shared governance, or to
5284 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012
complete rebuild. Some secondary schools ar e awaiting geotechnical information and a
range of options have been proffered to th em, but no firm proposal s or finite options
have been put on the table. We are still waiting to have those discussions. Of the 173
schools not affected by these firm proposals— that is, 80 percent—I announced that 40
would now begin repairs, that 23 school swimming pools would be completed by the
beginning of term 1, and that new provisi on would be made in Rolleston, Pegasus
Town, and Halswell. I also announced that there would be three advisory groups: an
education advisory board, a Wa itaha advisory board, and a Pasifika advisory board. I
announced a multidisciplined, fast-moving task  force that would be set up and would
include external expertise.
All of this was a nnounced to all schools,  in two consecutive groups, on Thursday.
The first group comprised those schools most directly affected. Every school was given
detailed information for their school and for the community cluster that they were a part
of. They were also given a time line and a process for engagement. They were given
contacts for the website, and the Ministry of Education has since followed up with a
discussion about when, over the next few days , to schedule a cluster meeting for them.
The time line for this third phase of cons ultation goes through to the middle of next
year, with more specific processes for differe nt schools, all of which will be advised to
those schools. It is quite understandable that  those communities most  directly affected
are upset. The challenge is providing certainty and clarity about the next steps. That is
what I have done. It will require us to work together, and the Ministry of Education has
been, or is in the process of being, in touc h with every school to schedule that ongoing
consultation.
I am proposing that of the 42 schools affect ed by closure or merger, 13 are proposed
to close. Of those, two have sought voluntary closure, five have rolls of fewer than 50,
and some have sustained earthquake damage a nd/or are in a cluster that has a range of
other options. I am proposing that 18 school s merge, of which two are kura kaupapa
Māori, both of which are in the south and are 5 kilometres apart, whilst there is no
Māori-medium option in the north. I am propos ing that five be replaced by one whole-
of-life campus with shared facilities in Aranui, and three share governance in Banks
Peninsula as an area school. Three are awai ting geotechnical inform ation. All of these
proposals are made in the context of a land and building assessment, movement of
people—before, now, and projected—educatio nal achievement, both pre-quake and
post-quake, diversity of provision across th e network, and a system-wide lift in
achievement.
At the centre of this $1 billion investment is a focus on the learner, now and in the
future, and on raising achievement for five out of five learners. I invite all the learning
community clusters to take full advantag e of the opportunities for engagement and
discussion in this third stage of consultation. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: I actually do not accept
that it is good enough for the Minister of E ducation to cancel a c onference that she was
due to attend tonight—

items.text: I didn’t cancel.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: She was supposed to be at the conference tonight—

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It was not my conference
and, therefore, it was not in my—

order. That is a debating point.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: It is not good enough that this Minister cancelled out of a

conference, and stand here in this House a nd not even complete the 15 minutes that has

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
