you.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: I do not believe that it is  good enough to stand in this
House and not acknowledge the impact th at this announcement—without warning,
without preparation to communities—has heaped upon those people who are suffering
down there as a result of the earthquake. In fact, what I really hear d the Minister say
was that this has given her an incredible  opportunity—that is what the earthquake has
given the Government—to do things that it would not otherwise be able to do. At the
launch we were told by the Government that Christchurch could be the exemplar for the
rest of New Zealand.
I want to put this on the record. The Government said that Christchurch would be the
exemplar for the rest of New Zealand. I belie ve that the rest of New Zealand needs to
hear what is going on in Christchurch. They ha ve to see this not as a Christchurch issue
but as a Government issue, where it is imposing its will on the people of Christchurch in
order to pilot the work that it wants to do in the rest of the country. This is not about just
Christchurch; this is coming to a school near  you. Every single New Zealander needs to
be aware of this.
I have to say that this is the message that is coming back from on the ground in
Christchurch at the moment as people reel  from the impact of that announcement.
Nothing prepared these communities for what they heard last Thursday.
The pre-breakfast cross-party forum from the Minister did not hing to prepare MPs
for what was to be announced that afternoon. Certainly, we were told about the clusters.
We were certainly told about shared site provision. In some instances we were told that
there would be some closures . But when we were told th at no thought whatsoever had
been given to preparing the community fo r the announcements—they talked about the
work that had been done with the schools only, not with the communities; they had
done no work with the communities to prepare them for the announcement on
closures—that was admitted at that meeting, and I guess that left us thinking that the
announcements were not going to be the way that they were. We believed that there
were going to be some sensible closures, some sensible mergers, and that they would be
the ones that have been sought. We have al ready heard that there are two schools that
are voluntarily going to seek closure in the time fr ame indicated by the Minister.
Everyone accepts there has to be change , but nothing prepared the people of
Christchurch for the change that this Government has wrought upon them.
Did the Minister give any thought to th e crushing blow that this announcement
would have on the parents and the children who have seen these schools as the mainstay
5286 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012
of their lives? I want  to remind this House that childre n were at schools in Christchurch
on the day of the earthquake, on 22 February, and those teachers and principals made
sure that there was somebody with the children all day until the parents could come. But
I know that there was a school where the pare nts never came, and that is because the
father was waiting in Latimer Square for hi s wife, who would never be pulled from the
CTV Building, and that is a school that is goi ng to close under the pr oposals if they are
adopted by this Government. I just want to remind this Ho use that there are people in
Christchurch who have absolutely depende d on the schools to give their children
normality and to give them the security of knowing that they are in safe hands while
their parents get on as best they can in terms of getting their own lives back to normal. It
has been a hard row to hoe, but I have to  say that the way this announcement was
announced was nothing less than cruel in terms of the impact it was going to have on
people.
What of the announcement itself? The day before we heard that confessed to by the
Minister in the House as she answered ques tions today, the princi pals of schools that
were going to close or merge—and, actuall y, remember that if 18 schools merge, it
means that nine schools close; so there are a hell of a lot more than 13 schools that are
going to close in Christchurch—got a phone cal l to come go a pre-launch briefing. So
they went to the pre-launch briefing, but be fore they went to the pre-launch briefing
they rang around to find out who got the in vitation to the pre- launch briefing, and it
started to emerge that, actually, maybe this  was not going to be quite what they
expected it to be. Was that part of the pl an? Did the Government want to create that
level of uncertainty so that  people whose schools were no t being merged or closed
would somehow defend the Government’s behaviour?
As people arrived at the meeting, they were  given name badges, and then we found
out that the colour of the name badge de scribed what was going to happen to their
school. This is how we treat principals and the chairs of boards of trustees. It is
absolutely outrageous how they were treated.
The Minister then gave a br iefing to this assembled grou p of principals and board
chairs, and she told them about the $1 billion to be invested in Ch ristchurch education.
She did not say how much of that was going to be poured into the redundancies that will
follow. She talked about the clusters and about how this was going to be a wonderful
opportunity. While she was speaking, they were distributing the packs to the teachers, to
the principals, and to the board trustees, and while they were sitting there hearing words
like “restore”, “consolidate”, and “rejuvenate”, they were reading their packs and their
packs were telling them that the words “r estore”, “consolidate”, and “rejuvenate”
actually were Government spin for “repair”, “merge”, and “close”—Government spin
for “repair”, “merge”, and “close”.
I think that the Minister ha s been genuinely surprised at the overwhelming response
of negativity from the people of Christchur ch, and she had to cancel her attendance at
this principals’ conference. She knew it was on. She knew it would be a clash with this
announcement, and that confirms to me the view  that she intended to release this at the
end of August but changed the launch date as a result of the interference from the office
of the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Reco very, and I am sure that he also advised
her how to run Government spin around a bad announcement. She knew that the
community would be looking for leadership at  this time from its school leaders. How
dare she treat communities like this—allowing the principals to be away at the time
when the community needs them the most? It is arrogance that beggars belief. And now
they are being led to believe that their views will count.
Well, I just remind this House what happene d when this House was asked to look at
Aorangi School. People will remember what  happened with Aorangi primary school
18 Sep 2012 Urgent Debates 5287
and how many of those students went to Burn side Primary School, in  the electorate of
the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery. How is he going to go and face those
parents and explain to them why he closed  this school and is now closing the school
where they have gone?
I find it unbelievable, reall y, that the Government has ta ken this approach. I do not
believe that the Government is really going to listen to the people at all, because the
Minister has made it cl ear that these are firm proposals. These schools are
predetermined. I want to remind the Minister that when a board wants to merge or close,
there are list of questions that the ministry asks the boards to consider. What educational
benefits for students would we hope to achieve ? Will there be educational and/or social
advantages for the students in a larger sc hool? How far away are neighbouring schools?
What travel would be involved for the st udents? Would these schools provide the
education the parents are seeking? What are the educational benefits?
These are the questions that we will be asking. I believe that Government members
have failed to stand in this urgent debate , which they said they were perfectly well
aware was going to happen today, and the Minister did not answer a single question that
her own ministry would ask a board to answer  before it would consider a merger or a
closure.
Everyone expects change to happen in Christ church; they do not expect a bombshell
like this to be dumped on a very, very damaged community.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I w ould just like to open by
acknowledging that this is a very, very difficult situation. It is difficult for Christchurch,
it is difficult for Waimakariri, and it is di fficult for all the areas of Selwyn that are
involved in this. It is difficu lt for the Government. It is di fficult for every single one of
us in Parliament to try to do the best by the people, the children, and the families in
Christchurch. But, unfortunately, I am going to have to say this was badly done, I say to
the Minister of Education. I do not know who advises you, ma’am, but again somebody
has advised you badly about how to actually communicate and consult with
communities.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Not the Chair.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: I beg your pardon, Mr Speaker. Somebody, Minister, has
advised badly on how to go about this process.
I want to take a moment to talk about the third round of consultation that the Minister
is talking about, and let us ju st talk about the first two r ounds of consultation. The word
“consultation” means to seek information a nd advice from, and to take into account
feelings and interests. The first tw o are quite clearly outlined in the Directions for
Education Renewal in Greater Christchurch . The first round of consultation involved
focus groups with invite d stakeholders. It is of interest—how wide did that stakeholder
invitation go? How many of the parents in these communities were invited to those
focus groups? Were they advertised in the pa per? Were they just the businesses? Were
the principals and the boards of trustees also  on that invitation list?  It would be nice to
know, Minister, because it is not actually documented inside this rather large document.
Obviously, you have very good staff to produ ce you a report, but not necessarily very
good staff to provide you with information about how to consult.
Then there was an online survey. So an on line survey—and we are just in the middle
of a digital literacy inquiry, actually—suggests that everybody has access to or the
ability to go online to complete a surve y. So that makes an assumption that all
demographics inside an incr edibly damaged area of New Zealand have access to get
online to complete this survey. It also begs the question: how was the fact that this
online survey was available for this input advertised? Were all the parents of these
schools given that information in the link to the survey through their school newsletters?
5288 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012
What is interesting is, of all the hundred s and hundreds of people who are affected by
this, the number of submissions received.
What is also interesting is the questions th at were asked. Some of them have nothing
to do with what it is that the Minister  announced the other day—useful information
perhaps, but they are included inside this  report and have no relevance. But one
question that is relevant, however, is questi on No. 8, which asks how important it is to
plan for fewer but larger schools where learners  may get a richer expe rience, even if it
means children may have to travel a bit furt her. This was the l east supported proposal
by every submitter. It was the most answered  question inside this survey from the
ministry. It was the least supported proposal. Yet, when it is dumped on these parents
and communities, this is actually probably one of the most strongly supported proposals
by the Government and by the Minister.
I would suggest that this statement that sits on the front of the Greater Christchurch

items.speaker: Information Pack
items.text: an opportunity plus innov ation to enhance education across Greater
Christchurch cannot be read in any other way than  that the Government has decided to
take a few ideas that some sort of elit e educationalists or members high up in the
ministry, sitting somewhere in the middle of Wellington, think would be a cool thing to
do, and has decided to launch it into this city. They may be  a very cool thing to do,
Minister. They may be some great ideas, but you have to extend the way you consult.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: I beg your pardon—the Minister must extend the way they
consult.
I think once again the Government ha s underestimated the connection that
communities have with their schools. Once again, it has underestimated the people of
Christchurch. They are realistic, the people of Christchurch. They have lived through
some disastrous times—a natural disaster, never witnessed before in my lifetime and in
the lifetime of most of the people in this Parliament. What held many of them together
was that sense of community. What happens ? We have seen it again and again and
again, when a Government—not necessarily this Government, but any Government—
has closed small schools, rural schools, ha s attacked class sizes , and has gone into
schools and, without widening out the consul tation beforehand and taking those parents
with them, has run into a brick wall. I can only suggest that the Government needs to
learn from the way that it does these things that  there is a better way, and it is to not run
a focus group and it is not to r un an online survey. It is to actually participate on a one-
on-one level and give the community some sense of real input that they might be able to
trust.
I also want to note that  the Minister, in a M āori Television intervie w last night, did
make mention that one of the criteria for some  of these schools that  have been selected
to close was based on academic performance. Th at is the first time, Minister, that we
actually start moving into this area. It is  well known among charter schools in America
that when there is a standa rdised testing regi me, if the school does not meet the
standardised testing regime then the St ate comes in and cl oses you down. What
happens, unfortunately, and why it is so pr evalent around people who believe in charter
schools, is because they believe that anot her private business will pop up and actually
fill that space.
But I also recognise that in the same interview on M āori Television the Minister
pooh-poohed the concerns by kura kaupapa that they would be merged into a single
charter school. The Minister, quite rightly, pointed out that that legislation around
charter schools has not come into this Hous e yet; therefore, there is no mechanism by
which a charter school can be formed. She is  quite right. But why should the people of
Christchurch take any comfort from that, Minister, consideri ng that just last week we
18 Sep 2012 Urgent Debates 5289
had the Advanced Technology Institute Bill that  needed to come into this House for its
first reading, but the establishment board  had already been established? The
Government continues to hold on to its one vot e majority in this House to force things
through. The fact that the legisl ation is not here yet is cold comfort. I think that the
Minister, her staff, and the ministry’s sta ff need to go out there and be an awful lot
clearer with regard to these communities and start building back up some trust.
Also, only in that last week, the ability to  have an elected body in the same area was
denied to them by another Minister in this House. So trust is pretty thin on the ground in
Christchurch. It is pretty thin on the ground, actu ally, in a lot of places throughout New
Zealand. I think that this could be improved. I am more than happy to sit down with the
Minister and help her to understand how that works—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have been very
tolerant with the member, but can I just a dvise her that every time she uses the word
“you”, she brings the Chair into the debate. She may not do that.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: My apologies, Mr Speaker. I will try harder.
There is one other little thing, and that is the billion dollars that is mentioned at the
beginning of the opportunity plus  innovation pack, and that is great. That is wonderful.
The Government is investing up to $1 bi llion over 10 years to  develop Greater
Christchurch. I have a question. Is this th e same billion dollars that the rest of New
Zealand has been told will be spent on them and their schools and their hospitals, or is
this another billion dollars being taken out of  the future fund? Again, it is not clear,
Minister. So there is an awful lot of informa tion that has not been clear. If it is not clear
to members of the House, how can it be clear to the parents, the children, the principals,
and the boards of trustees that this is going to affect?
I think, in closing, the only other comment I would like to make is that it is all very
well and good to send out a le tter on 5 September, an email on 6 September, and to
follow up with a phone call on 13 September to the chairmen of the boards of trustees.
These people, predominantly, are also in em ployment. They have jobs and real lives
that they go on with, while giving their evenings and what time they can to fulfil this
governance role to their communities. To say to them that, by the way, there is a
meeting in 8 day’s time at 10 a.m. in the mo rning that you need to take time off work
for—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: —sorry—and that it was requi red of them to take time off
work to attend is, I think, outsi de the bounds of reality, Minist er. I think it is very hard.
This message has been badly delivere d—incredibly badly delivered—and, really,
whoever is advising the Minister needs to do better.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker, ka
nui te mihi ki a koe otirā, ki a tātou o te Whare i tēnei rā. Ko te nuinga o ngā kōrero kua
korero kētia e wētāhi, ā, nō reira ka waiho ake ērā kōrero kia iri i te pakitara-ā-Whare. E
hāngai tonu ana waku k ōrero ki ngā mea, me k ī, kua puta i roto i ng ā kōrero o ngā mea
o roto i ng ā kura kaupapa M āori. Me taku m ōhio an ō hoki kei te ng ākaunui t ō tātou
Minita ki te āhuatanga o te kura kaupapa M āori. Kua mōhio tonu ia ki ng ā piki me ng ā
heke e p ā ana ki ng ā kura kaupapa M āori nō reira, ko āku kōrero he mea whakat ūpato
noa ake, ka mutu, ko ngā kōrero kua puta mai ki ngā taringa o te Pāti Māori inā tata nei.
Nō reira, me pēnei rawa te k ōrero, wā poto i muri o te putanga o te k ōrero i roto o
Ōtautahi, kua āhua rerekē te noho o ngā kura i roto o t ērā takiwā. I tae mai tētahi īmēra,
i t ētahi o ng ā mātua o roto o te kura kaupapa M āori o Te Wh ānau Tahi. Ko Melanie
Rīwai Couch te ingoa o te wahine nei, anā, i pātai a ia i ētahi pātai. Anei tana kōrero i te
reo P ākehā: “The two kura each have a very di stinct and unique history, and, while
supportive of each other, any talk of me rger spells a death knell to any M āori school.
5290 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012
The earthquakes are just a cover and local M āori families committed to Te Reo M āori
are likely to be the ones to pay for this experiment. Whatever happened to partnership,
protection, and participation?”. Koi nei te ia o tana kōrero. Ka mutu, koi nā tana kōrero.
Kua oti i te mema a Catherin e Delahunty te whakaara ake i ētahi o ngā take kua puta
mai i roto i ng ā kōrero ēngari, tērā pea e rua ng ā take nui. Tuatahi, ko te w ā kōrerorero
mō te take nei, me k ī i te reo P ākehā, ko te consultation, ā, kua rongo ng ā taringa o te
Minita i ia e k ōrero ana m ō te tekau m ā marama pea, e k ōrerohia ana. H āunga t ērā
kōrero ka mutu, me kī , kua oti kē i a ia, otirā, Te Tāhuhu o te Mātauranga, te whakatau
i te huarahi ka whaiwhai haeretia e ng ā kura ā ngā tau kai mua i te aroaro. E ai ki te
Melanie Couch nei he huarahi t ēnei, me k ī, e wh āia ana hei whakakotahi nei, an ō nei e
ōrite ana ngā kura e rua ēngari, ko tā rātou he kī atu, me kī, ko ngā mea o roto i ngā kura
e rua, ēhara. He rerekē anō ngā kura. Ā, tēnā kura me ōna kōrero, me tōna wairua. Tērā
kura me ōna kōrero, me tōna wairua.
Nō reira, ko tā mātou te Pāti Māori ko te k ī atu, āe, kāre ā mātou raruraru ki te whai
atu i t ētahi huarahi hai whakapakari ake i Te Reo M āori, te wairua M āori, te ng ākau
Māori, te tikanga M āori hei oranga m ō te painga o ng ā tamariki, otir ā, ng ā wh ānau i
roto i ngā kura. Ko te mate k ē i Ōtautahi e ai ki t ā mātau e rongo nei, tuatahi, k āre te rū
o roto o Ōtautahi i pā ki ngā kura, kātahi ka rua, kai te pai r ātau. Kua kī, e ai ki t ā rātau
ēhara i te mea kua puta te nuinga ki w āhi kē. He aha te take kua p ā mai Te T āhuhu o te
Mātauranga ki te kī atu, ā, me whakakotahi nei kōrua nā runga i te āhuatanga o te rū. Ko
tā rātau ko te kī atu ē kāo, kāre i te tika. Ko tētahi i roto i Te Kura Whakapumau i te Reo
Tūturu ki Waitaha, i k ī mai ia, tino ohorere ia n ā runga i te kore k ōrero a t ētahi ki a
rātau. Māna tena e whakautu, māna tēnā e kōrero.
Ko t ētahi o ng ā take nui kua puta mai, ko te k ī a ētahi o roto i ng ā kura kaupapa
Māori, he huarahi tēnei ki te kura h ōu, arā, ko te kura h ōu rua, arā, ko te charter school.
Kāre au i te tino m ōhio, āe rānei, kāre rānei ēngari, tērā kōrero, anā, kua tāpirihia atu ki
ngā kōrero o te whakakotahitanga i ngā kura, kai reira tonu tētahi raruraru nui. Ēhara i te
mea, kai te whakaae atu r ānei, kei te whakahē rānei i tērā huarahi, mā tēnā iwi, mā tēnā
hapū tērā e k ōrero. Mēnā koi r ā te huarahi e hiahiatia nei e Ng āi Tahu. Ka pai, wh āia
atu. Ēngari, ēhara i te mea e p ēnei, e pērā. Me whai atu i ng ā huarahi e rua, mēnā koi rā
tā rātau e pīrangi nei, kura kaupapa Māori, āe, kura reorua, kai a rātau tērā.
Nā, hei whakamutu i taku k ōrero, e rua noa iho ng ā kura kaupapa M āori o roto o
Ōtautahi. Ar ā nō ng ā kura reorua kei St Albans, kei Richmond, kei Rowley, kei
Woolston anō hoki. Ko te mate k ē, e rua noa iho ng ā kura kai t ērā takiwā. Ahakoa, he
tokomaha tonu ng ā Māori kei t ērā takiw ā e noho ana. Ki te whakakotahi nei, ki te
whakakao nei i ng ā kura e rua nei, ka whakaaro ake, āe rānei, ka tipu ko t ēnei mea te
kura kaupapa Māori ā ngā tau. Ko wai ka mōhio?
Ka mutu, ko te kupu whakamutunga, ko tērā i puta i a Mark Solomon, ko tana kī mai,
kai te noho āwangawanga ia mō te huarahi e whai haeretia ana e r ātau. Ko tana k ī mai:
“[We] support the extension of M āori-medium education th roughout Christchurch and
any reduction in services would be in consistent with this kaupapa,”. N ō reira, me kī ko
Ngāi Tahu kai roto i ng ā whiriwhiringa katoa, te t ūmanako ia ka aro mai te Minita, ka
mutu, te tāhuhu ki ēnei manawapā kua puta i roto o te hapori o Ōtautahi. Kia ora tātau.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and a huge acknowledgment to you, and, indeed, to all of
us in the House today. Most of the issues have been addressed already by some, and so I
will leave those sentiments hanging there on the walls of the House. My comments will
focus on things that came out of what those involved in M āori-medium schools have
stated, knowing full well that our Minist er of Education is passionate about the
situation relating to M āori-medium schools. She underst ands the ups and downs that
Māori-medium schools experience, so my sentim ents are merely of a cautionary nature
and about what the Māori Party has heard just recently.
18 Sep 2012 Urgent Debates 5291

items.speaker: So let me put it this way
items.text: in a short s pace of time following the announcement of the
Christchurch plan, the plight of kura in that area has changed somewhat. An email
arrived from one of the parents involved with Te Kura Kaupapa M āori o te Wh ānau
Tahi. Melanie R īwai Couch is the name of this woman. Now she really asked some
searching questions. Here is what she said in English: “The two kura each have a very
distinct and unique history, and, while supporti ve of each other, any talk of merger
spells a death knell to any M āori school. The earthquakes ar e just a cover and local
Māori families committed to Te Reo M āori are likely to be the ones to pay for this
experiment. Whatever happened to partnership, protection, and participation?”. That is
the gist of her comments, and that is what she said.
The member Catherine Delahunty has already  brought up some of the issues that
have emerged from some of the talk, but th ere are two major issues, perhaps. Firstly,
the kōrerorero about this issue—the consultation, perhaps, in English. The Minister has
heard, as she was talkin g, that the consultations will be  for 18 months. That aside, the
second major issue is that sh e, and, indeed, the Ministry  of Education, have already
determined the future merging process that the two kura will follow. To Melanie Couch,
this merging process to be followed by th e two kura makes the assumption that the two
schools are similar, but they are not. They ar e telling the Government that each kura is
distinctly different to the other. The st ories and spirituality about each one are quite
different.
We the M āori Party are saying, yes, we do not  have a problem pursuing a process
that will strengthen M āori language, spirituality, feel ings, and culture for the well-
being and benefit of children, and, indeed, of families in both kura. The problem really
in Christchurch, according to what we he ard, is that the Christchurch earthquake did
not affect either kura. That is the first thing. The second is that they are fine. To them, it
is not as though the majority of students moved to some other place. Why has the
Ministry of Education contacted and told them that your two kura must merge due to the
earthquake? They have said, no, that is not right. A person from Te Kura Whakapumau
i te Reo T ūturu ki Waitaha said to us that he was really shocked because no one spoke
to them. No one said: “I will respond to that. I will speak to you about that.”
One of the big issues that emerged was the speculation by some in M āori-medium
schools that this is an avenue towards a new school, a new merged school: the charter
school. I do not know for sure whether it is ye s or no, but that is the talk, and it adds to
the statements for the two kura to merge into one, and that brings up another big
problem. It is not as though one  agrees or disagrees to that avenue. It is for that tribe
and subtribe to determine. If  that is the way that Ng āi Tahu want to go, well and good,
go for it. But it is not saying this or t hat one in particular. They must pursue both
avenues if this is what they want; Māori-medium schools or bilingual schools, that is up
to them.
To end my address, there are only two Māori-medium schools in Christchurch, and a
bilingual school at St Albans, Richmond, Ro wley, and also Woolston. The problem is
that there are only two kura in that  area, despite the large number of M āori living
there. To merge or gather these two kura together, the thinking might be, yes, this thing
called a Māori-medium school might grow in years to come. Who is to know that?
In the end the final word might be that  which Mark Solomon expressed when he
alluded to the fact that he was somewhat c oncerned at the path that was being pursued.

items.speaker: He said
items.text: “[We] suppor t the extension of M āori-medium education throughout
Christchurch and any reduction in services w ould be inconsistent with this kaupapa,”.
So let us assume that Ngāi Tahu is participating in all negotiations. The hope is that the
Minister and eventually the ministry take heed of the concerns that have come out of the
Christchurch community. My appreciation to us all.]
5292 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to make a
brief contribution to this debate on the announcement of the rearrangement of schools in
Christchurch. Can I say on behalf of the Labour education team that we want to
acknowledge the stress that the schools, the teachers, the pr incipals, the boards, and the
kids have been under since the earthquake. Regardless of where we stand on this
particular announcement, I am sure we can all agree that the schools have done an
absolutely wonderful and commendable job—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: And early childhood education services.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: —I am going to come to the early childhood education services
in a minute—of supporting kids through a re ally difficult couple of years that, you
know, they have experienced down in Christ church. As my colleague Sue Moroney has
pointed out, the early childhood centres have also done an absolutely wonderful job. I
guess for those of us living outside of Christchurch it is difficult to comprehend in some
respects the difficulty that schools would have with not knowing where parents are and
not being able to contact parents. It is the same with early childhood services. They
have done an absolutely wonderful job, and I do want to acknowledge the contribution
that they have made in that regard.
I am concerned that this announcement goes a little bit further, potentially, than what
some would have been expecting. I do not th ink that anyone would have expected that
there would not be change required in Ch ristchurch following the earthquakes. They
have had a significant impact on the whole community and on the educational
community, as well. I think everybody expected that change was going to come and that
it was going to be required. Th e extent of these changes, however, is larger than what
people anticipated, and I think that it creates a lot more anxiety for people when they
hear the changes proposed in Ch ristchurch being referred to as exemplars for the rest of
the country. I think it would be very unfair on the people of Christchurch that they be
used as guinea pigs for experimenting with  different models of education, at a time
when they are already under significant strai n. I am concerned that elements of what is
being proposed by the Government  certainly would suggest th at that is the case. The
Government appears to be using the cover of the earthquake to trial things that it cannot
do elsewhere, and I actually think that is very, very unfair on the people of
Christchurch—I think it is very unfair on the people of Christchurch.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: So rubbish.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: If the Government—and Gerry Brownlee says it is rubbish—
wants to do things in Christchurch that it is not willing to do el sewhere, it should be
upfront and honest about it. It  should actually say to the pe ople of Christchurch “Hey,
look. We’re going to experiment with the futu re of the kids in Christchurch to see
whether this actually works.”, because that is effectively what the announcements it has
made amount to. It is going to experiment on the children of Christchurch, and I do not
think that is the right thing to do. You know , some change is required, and I have
acknowledged that some change is required, but the Government could at least get the
process around that right—it c ould at least make sure it gets the process around that
right.
When principals are saying that teachers in their schools were getting text messages
saying that their school is being closed while they were still in the meeting being briefed
about it, and hearing about it, and they were not actually in the school s and able to talk
to the teachers concerned, that suggests that  the process was a complete botch-up—that
suggests that the process was a complete botch-up. Giving people colour-coded name
tags indicating whether their school was going to close or merge or be pushed out of
existence is absolutely disgraceful. That is not the way people should be treated. The
18 Sep 2012 Urgent Debates 5293
Government could have at least afforded so me dignity to the process, which clearly it
did not in that regard.
Giving people colour-coded name badges to indicate whether or not their school was
going to be closed, like naughty primary school kids, is absolutely disgraceful. I am not
surprised, though. I am not surpri sed, given the Minister who ha s been placed in charge
of it. She cannot seem to manage to make any announcement without absolutely
hashing it up, although she seems to be better at backtracking than making
announcements. So when she comes back to backtrack on all of these proposals, I am
sure she will probably get that a little b it better than her initial announcement, and she
might have learnt something from the pr ocess. Then maybe when the backtrack
comes—the flip-flop comes—maybe she will finally get the process right around that,
because she certainly has not got the process right around this.
Finally, to conclude, this is not an opportunity for the G overnment to inflict charter
schools with unregistered teachers on the stud ents of Christchurch, who are already
dealing with enough challenges w ithout having the Government decide that it is going
to trial its ideological charter schools experiment, which has been proven to fail
everywhere else around the worl d it has been tried. This is  not an opportunity for the
Government to experiment on the kids of Christchurch. It needs to go back to the
drawing board and get a process right that is fair, that is open, a nd that is honest about
what it is trying to achieve, because it certainly has not been in this process.

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: As one of the speakers in
this House who actually comes from Canterbu ry and comes from Christchurch, it is
really interesting to see t hose who cannot even pronounce the names of the schools, let
alone know what it is like to live through ear thquakes, try to make some comment of
any worth in this House. It would be a grea t thing if the educatio n of our kids and our
grandkids could be put above politics, but what happens now in Christchurch is it is not.
We get accused of some sort of breach of  the embargo. It was not the Government
that breached the embargo—it was not the Government that breached the embargo. We
were not responsible for that  breach of the embargo. Yes, it was unfortunate, but if we
put it in perspective, we have lost 4,500 lear ners in Canterbur y—in Waimakariri,
Christchurch, and Selwyn. There are 4,500 learners who have gone somewhere else, and
if the members on the other side believe that  the loss of 4,500 learners means that it is
just business as usual, then there is no wonder that they are st ill on those Opposition
benches.
We also talk about consultation. How many times have we heard that this has been
out for consultation? This is not the first round of consultation. This  is not the second
round of consultation. This is the third round of consultation, and it is still happening.
Having said that, there is still, even after all these months in Christchurch, an underlying
fragility about the people of Canterbu ry—about the people of Christchurch,
Waimakariri, and Selwyn. These are still challenging times. Change is difficult and we
acknowledge that. We also acknowledge that th e schools have been fantastic in being a
rock for some of those kids, for giving them some sense of stability and some sense of
normality. Of course change is difficult, but when we lose 4,500 learners, something
simply has to happen.
I would like to mention some welcom e news from the announcement. In
Waimakariri we have been waiting for a l ong time for the announcement that we would
get a new school, and now we get a new school in Pegasus.  We have a new subdivision
there with an extra 1,800 homes and an incr eased population of 4,700 residents. Yes, it
means the closure of Waikuku School, but fo r those who do not live in the area,
Waikuku School has actually been wanting to close and shift to Pegasus for some time
now. It has not only outgrown its premises, it has outgrown its parking, it has outgrown
5294 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012
its drop-off and pick-up areas, and it has out grown its septic tank requirements. So for
them the announcement of a new primary school for Pegasus town will bring relief to
the parents, the primary school’s children, an d the community in that electorate. We
have been waiting for that for some time and that is certainly some welcome news.
I just want to make one mention, and it mi ght be a wee bit off topic, that private
schools in our area have also been impacted, yet Labour hates private schools. The only
thing I can think of as to why it hates priv ate schools is that private schools gave it
Michael Cullen. But private schools have  been damaged and impacted by the
earthquake. My own school has no chapel , no dining room, no science block, no arts
block, and no swimming pool. The students have been in marquees since the
earthquake. Do they complain? No. Do th ey get criticised by the Opposition? Yes.
Private schools also provide fantastic education for our schools in Christchurch.
It would be wonderful if this could be seen as an opportunity to have a world-leading
education system in Canterbury—not guinea pi gs; actual improvement to have a world-
leading education system in Canterbury, Wa imakariri, Selwyn, and Christchurch, and
not just as an opportunity for that side of the House to us e its union mates to incite
protests and rallies. Our kids are better than that and our kids deserve be tter than that.
Education is above politics—it is above politics, and so it should be.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: I am pleased that we have
had the chance to have this debate in th e House today actually, because, for one, I am
getting heartily tired of all the misinformation, scaremongering, and drivel coming from
stirrers in the Opposition parties and certain other interest groups in this sector. Like my
colleague who has just resumed her seat, Kate Wilkinson, it is pretty hard to sit in this
House and hear speaker after speaker from  the Opposition benche s, who do not come
from Canterbury and who are not living w ith the situation, st and up and, frankly,
patronise the people of Canterbury and those of us who are working very hard to try not
only to repair and rebuild what we have bu t also to take the opportunity that this
horrible, horrible set of circumstances has given us, and promise the people of
Canterbury not just to put back what we had but to build something far, far better.
The earthquakes changed our lives and th ey changed our landscape. There is no
question about that. We all know that the difficulties did not end with the Portaloos, the
liquefaction, and the demolition. These difficu lties are real, we are living them every
day, and they will continue while we go through this rebuild period. But the one thing
that we hold on to—the one thing that makes this bearable for us in Canterbury—is that
we have a vision of a city that  we are going to get from th is process. We are going to
have the best small city in the world, as Minister Brownlee has to ld us. The people of
Selwyn and Waimakariri, who share in the futu re of Christchurch City, know that and
the people of Christchurch know that. The opportun ity for us now is to take this terrible
tragedy that has happened to us and build fr om it, and to offer our citizens the chance
not just to go back to what we had but to build something fa r, far better. That is what
my colleague Minister Parata has been working at ever since she took the portfolio, and,
before her, Minister Tolley.
I have sat in numerous meetings where I have heard Opposition members and
stakeholder groups complain that it was all taking too long a nd that what our
community wants is answers. So what di d Ms Parata and Minister Brownlee announce
last week? Well, first and foremost, they announced a billion-dollar investment into
education in Canterbury—a b illion-dollar investment. They  announced that 173 of the
215 schools could get on with some certainty. Let us not forget that. I have had a
number of emails from principals in my el ectorate thanking us for that. One principal
emailed me last week and said he wanted  to pass on his thanks. He said it was a
landmark day for his school and his community, and that finally getting word that the
18 Sep 2012 Urgent Debates 5295
rebuild would be happening in the imme diate future was truly amazing; it was
unbelievable. Another has emailed me to say th at the news that th e school was going to
be repaired was received with great relief and celebration.
I am not saying this to diminish the diffi culties for the 20-odd schools that are in a
period of uncertainty. I do not want to di minish that for a minute. I know those
communities will find this very tough to work  through, and we are going to be helping
them every step of the way. But let us reme mber that these are proposals. They are
proposals. At some point, you have to come up  with a set of ideas, you have to talk to
the community about them, and if the community  thinks there is a better way of dealing
with the challenges we face, then of course we will listen to that.
Let us reflect on a couple of things in this . As well as the 173 schools that have had
their futures confirmed, 40 of them can get on with fast-track re building projects, and

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Burnham?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: —I said Burnham, Mr Cosg rove, if you were listening—

items.text: I, for one, accept, as do other

have waited. But it is good news—and I wanted something positive—that finally the
Government has reinstated the money and the school is going to move to Pegasus Bay.
5296 Urgent Debates 18 Sep 2012

with that proposition. At Ōuruhia School, where I wa s last night with other

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I
want to start by acknowledging the move r of this motion, Catherine Delahunty. I
thought she really did do a good job of indi cating, firstly, that this was a serious
problem that had to be dealt with, that there were emotions that needed to be considered
in all of this, and that ther e was no particular easy way of  going about it, but also that
there were, perhaps, some things that coul d be done better as we progress through the
consultation period. I think that as a discussion  topic for this House, a debate in this
House is perfectly appropriate, and I thank her for the tone of her contribution.
There has been nothing particularly easy a bout the last 2 years of dealing with the
fallout from the earthquake events in Cant erbury. There is no particular decision that
has come naturally and simply. Every one of them has required a great deal of
consideration and a great deal of thought about the best in terests of the people who are
most affected. I want to say to some of the other speakers who have spoken this
afternoon specifically about cases they are familiar with, such as the M āori immersion

schools having to come together, that none of th at is something that we want to do. It is
something that has been put upon us by the ci rcumstance and has to be considered. That
is part of this process today.
Ms Martin, from the New Zealand First Party, made a number of interesting
comments. Firstly, she said that there wa s too much information prepared but not
enough consultation. Well, I do not know how you have consultation without significant
amounts of information being given to peopl e. Further to that, I do not know how the
Government was supposed to talk to 500 indi viduals, so 250 principals and 250 chairs
of boards, and then all of the people who support them, the staff of all those schools,

This is a difficult, difficult process. No one is denying that, and I am grateful that all
other members have acknowledged that. I do want to say, though, to people who are
listening that there is no part of the city th at is immune from the considerations that
have had to be put forward in this process. In my own electorate in the north-west there
are three schools that face the possibility of being closed. Those schools are in relatively
close proximity to each other, and there are numerous schools around and about. It
simply indicates that the demographic in Christchurch has shif ted quite significantly.
The growth patterns for the city have cha nged and have moved, and it would be plain
irresponsible to go around saying to every school “Look, we’re going to come along and
fix everything up, and then take  a longer period of time to sort all this out.” The one
thing that people in Canterbury apprecia te most is decisi ons. They do not like
indecision, and the only way that we could get to a decision point in this was to put it all
on the table for that wide consideration.
I have to say that I am utterly disgusted at some of the cynical manipulation of what I
think is genuine anxiety, for what our oppon ents, particularly in the Labour Party,
perceive as being to their political a dvantage. There is no—no—winning in getting
alongside people who are deeply distressed an d telling them that they do not have to
deal with the problem that is in front of them , that they should not have to deal with the
problem, or that if only there was someone else running things th e problem would not
be there in the first place. That is not true , and I have got to say that we have been
through land decisions where we have had the same rhet oric blown out from Mr
Cosgrove, all about “I’m here for my local  community. I’m an advocate. I won’t be
deterred.” All that does is reinforce the angst, anguish, and hurt that people are having
to suffer. It is disgraceful and it is time it stopped, because this country has never, ever
dealt with a problem as big as this. It is very easy for the rest of New Zealand to think
that it has been 2 years and it should have gone away, but , for goodness’ sake, this is a
huge problem. We are tackling it in as smooth a way as is possible. Yes, there will be
some people who do not like the way we are handling it. That is what it is all about.
But what I can say in this case is that 173 schools out of 215 got the green light the
other day to go ahead, repair, and get on with things. That is overwhelmingly positive. It

ENVIRONMENT CANTERBURY (TEMPORARY COMMISSIONERS AND
IMPROVED WATER MANAGEMENT) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I move, That the
Environment Canterbury (Temporary Commissioners and Improved Water
Management) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Local
Government and Environment Committee to cons ider the bill. At the appropriate time I
intend to move that the committee present its final report to the House on or before 30
January 2013.
The Canterbury region is of national sign ificance. It has over 60 percent of New
Zealand’s freshwater resource. It has around 34 percent of New Zealand’s hydro
generation capacity and 70 percent of its ge neration storage, and accounts for in the
order of 18 percent of the country’s overa ll hydroelectric gene ration. The region has
huge economic growth potential and is a key driver in making New Zealand a more
productive and competitive economy. It is v ital that a clear vision is developed for
economic growth and sustainable manageme nt of the natural resources in the
Canterbury region. To do this, the Canterbury region needs l eadership that is effective
in its planning and decision making, leader ship that works in  a constructive and
collaborative manner with councils, iwi, and other key stakeholders, and leadership that
inspires confidence throughout our Canterbur y community. This bill provides for the
continuation—

5302 Env. Canterbury (Temp. Commissioners etc.) Amdt Bill 18 Sep 2012
